unit.title: Teaching embedded and IoT systems at university

lesson.title: Sampling, Nyquist and the ADC
lesson.subtitle: From a real signal to numbers

video.title: Sampling, Nyquist and the ADC: From a real signal to numbers
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Joseph - computer science lecturer, Nairobi
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

scenes.narration: My students built a pulse monitor that showed twelve beats a minute on a healthy volunteer. The circuit was fine. They were sampling a fast signal far too slowly.
Today: how a sensor signal becomes numbers, why sampling too slowly invents fake frequencies, and how many bits you really need.
An analogue to digital converter measures a voltage at regular instants. The sampling rate is how many measurements per second. Between samples, the converter sees nothing.

Shannon's sampling theorem says a signal with no frequencies above B can be rebuilt exactly from samples taken faster than two B per second. Sample slower, and high frequencies fold down as fake low ones. That is aliasing.
Mains hum is fifty hertz. Sampled sixty times a second, it appears as a slow ten hertz wave. Sampled at a thousand, it appears correctly as fifty.

An n-bit converter splits its range into two to the n levels. A ten-bit converter on three point three volts has steps of about three millivolts. Each extra bit halves the step and adds about six decibels.
Students treat sampling as a software setting. Show a spinning wheel under a strobe light, or a film of car wheels turning backwards. They see aliasing before they see the maths.
Quick check! A vibration sensor must capture frequencies up to four hundred hertz. What is the lowest sampling rate that can work in theory?
Just above eight hundred samples per second. In practice engineers sample several times faster and put an anti-aliasing filter in front of the converter.
In the app, open the converter lab. Change the sampling rate and the number of bits, and watch the rebuilt signal improve or fall apart.
Your turn. A twelve-bit converter has a reference of four point zero nine six volts. What is the size of one step?
One millivolt, because two to the twelve is four thousand and ninety six. Remember: sample faster than twice the highest frequency, filter first, and each bit halves the step.

scenes.on_screen_text: Try it in your next lab
scenes.narration: Try it in your next lab: have pairs sample a signal generator at five rates on a microcontroller. They plot what they see and predict each alias before measuring it.

checkpoints.prompt: A sensor must capture up to 400 Hz. Lowest sampling rate that can work in theory?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: the rate must exceed 2B = 800 Hz.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: Nyquist needs more than twice the highest frequency, 2 × 400 = 800 Hz.

checkpoints.prompt: A 12-bit ADC has a 4.096 V reference. Size of one step?
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: 2¹² = 4,096 levels, so 4.096 V / 4,096 = 1 mV.
